title: Exploring hydrogen pipeline costs by considering regional geographical and political characteristics - Nature Energy
gist: A GIS-based global study of 4,900 potential hydrogen pipeline routes finds the levelized cost of transport varies by a factor of three (10.9 to 34.2 EUR/MWh per 1,000 km straight-line) once terrain, land use, population density, sea depth and country-specific WACC are modelled, versus the uniform 1.20-1.40 detour factor used in most energy system studies. Rerunning European models with route-specific costs changes hydrogen flows on 83-93% of corridors, discards some routes entirely and reverses at least one trade direction, despite transport being only a small share of delivered hydrogen cost.

themes.theme: Hydrogen pipeline buildout scale and FID gap

insights.claim: Global hydrogen pipeline length is projected to rise from roughly 5,000 km today to 19,000 km by 2030, 37,000 km by 2035 and 209,000 km by 2050, a more than fortyfold expansion of a niche asset class.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Sizes a multi-decade pipeline EPC, steel and compressor capex cycle; the 2030-2035 step is where order books would first have to inflect.
insights.quote: from around 5,000 km today to 19,000 km by 2030 and 37,000 km by 2035
insights.locator: Main: 'The total length of hydrogen pipelines is expected to increase substantially'

insights.claim: Only 6% of announced hydrogen projects have reached a final investment decision, so the entire pipeline demand forecast rests on an announcement pipeline that has overwhelmingly not been financed.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The single most important sanity check on hydrogen infrastructure forecasts; track FID conversion rate, not announcement volume.
insights.quote: only 6% of announced projects have reached a final investment decision
insights.locator: Main: 'These complex challenges are even underlined by the high uncertainty'

insights.claim: About a quarter of estimated global hydrogen demand is expected to be traded and transported internationally, meaning most hydrogen is consumed near where it is made and cross-border transport infrastructure serves a minority of volume.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Caps the addressable market for international hydrogen transport assets; local production plus local offtake remains the dominant structure.
insights.quote: Approximately a quarter of the estimated global hydrogen demand is expected to be traded and transported internationally
insights.locator: Main: opening paragraph on hydrogen as a critical energy carrier

insights.claim: The regions identified as probable hydrogen importers are Germany, the Netherlands, Japan and South Korea, concentrating import-infrastructure demand in four industrial economies with limited domestic renewable resource.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Import terminal, pipeline and shipping demand concentrates in these four buyers; their policy and subsidy decisions set the global trade structure.
insights.locator: Discussion: 'existing work on hydrogen imports to regions that will probably need them'

themes.theme: The uniform detour factor is empirically wrong

insights.claim: Standard cost estimates multiply a straight-line distance by a detour factor of 1.20 to 1.40 and a flat distance-specific cost, a heuristic that ignores every region-specific characteristic of the actual corridor.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Any hydrogen cost model you are handed probably embeds this heuristic; ask which detour factor was used before trusting the delivered cost.
insights.quote: Typical values for detour factors on international routes range from 1.20 to 1.40
insights.locator: Main: 'For new pipelines with unknown routes and distances'

insights.claim: Real-world detour factors span 1.00 to 4.76, with existing global oil and gas transmission lines clustering at an interquartile range of 1.05 to 1.35 while the proposed European Hydrogen Backbone clusters far higher at 1.54 to 1.82.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Planned European hydrogen corridors already detour ~50% more than historical oil and gas lines, so EHB cost estimates built on 1.2-1.4 are structurally too low.
insights.quote: The interquartile range of the detour factors of these real-world projects ranges from 1.05 to 1.35 for GEM data and from 1.54 to 1.82 for EHB data
insights.locator: Fig. 1 discussion: 'The detour factors are calculated as the ratio of the actual pipeline distance'

insights.claim: For 48% of modelled routes even the upper literature factor of 1.40 is an underestimate, and 61% of all routes fall outside the conventional 1.20-1.40 band in one direction or the other.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Roughly half of hydrogen corridor cost estimates in circulation are optimistic; the error is not symmetric noise but a systematic bias on most routes.
insights.quote: For many routes (48%), even a factor of 1.40 (that is, the higher value used in literature) proves to be an underestimation.
insights.locator: Section 'Influence of detour and geographical characteristics'

insights.claim: High total cost factors are driven by either a high geographic cost factor or a high detour factor but rarely both, producing an L-shaped scatter, because a route can usually buy its way around bad terrain by going further or accept the terrain and stay short.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A useful diagnostic: if a project claims both a short route and easy terrain in a hard region, the cost estimate is probably missing something.
insights.quote: high total factors are primarily driven by either a high cost factor or a high detour factor but rarely both
insights.locator: Fig. 4 discussion: 'The scatter plot indicates that high total factors'

insights.claim: Total factors reach 3.63 in North America and 1.93 in South America, while in Europe and South America they essentially never fall below 1.1, meaning the conventional band brackets neither the best nor the worst cases.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Worst-case North American corridors cost nearly 3x the planning assumption; route-level diligence is required before committing capital.
insights.locator: Section 'Influence of detour and geographical characteristics'

insights.claim: Five short Chinese routes under 250 km straight-line distance produced total factors of up to 7 because they were forced through densely populated locations, and had to be excluded from the analysis as outliers.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Dense-corridor hydrogen distribution in Asian megaregions can be an order of magnitude more expensive than headline numbers suggest.
insights.locator: Fig. 3 caption: 'Five short (<250 km straight-line) routes in China'

themes.theme: Global cost dispersion and regional ranking

insights.claim: Modelled levelized cost of hydrogen pipeline transport ranges from 10.9 to 34.2 euros per MWh of hydrogen per 1,000 km of straight-line distance, a nearly threefold spread between the cheapest and most expensive corridor globally.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The three-times spread is the headline number for screening which export corridors can ever be competitive on delivered hydrogen cost.
insights.quote: The LCOT ranges from 10.9 to 34.2 euros per megawatt-hour of hydrogen for every 1,000 km
insights.locator: Section 'Regional variation in hydrogen pipeline costs'

insights.claim: Europe, North America and Asia have mean transport costs of 15.0, 15.6 and 16.2 EUR/MWh per 1,000 km respectively, while Africa at 17.2 and South America at 17.1 are structurally more expensive per unit distance.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Africa and South America, the presumed low-cost hydrogen producers, carry a transport cost penalty that partly offsets cheap renewables.
insights.locator: Section 'Regional variation in hydrogen pipeline costs'

insights.claim: Europe's cost distribution is tight with a standard deviation of 1.5 while North America's is the widest at 4.2, containing both the cheapest and most expensive routes in the world.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: In Europe an average assumption is roughly safe; in North America route selection dominates the economics and averages are useless.
insights.locator: Section 'Regional variation in hydrogen pipeline costs'

insights.claim: Most routes cluster between 12.7 and 18.6 EUR/MWh per 1,000 km with a global standard deviation of 2.9, so the extreme values are genuine tails rather than a broad flat distribution.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A central case near 15 EUR/MWh per 1,000 km is defensible for screening, but tail routes must be identified individually.
insights.locator: Fig. 2 caption: 'The histogram depicts the global distribution of LCOTs'

insights.claim: Where pipeline costs are below average, pipelines hold a clear advantage over shipping, and where they are above average the economics shift toward shipping or alternative carriers, making transport mode a regional rather than a global technology choice.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The pipeline-versus-ammonia-shipping debate has no universal winner; corridor-level cost data decides which carrier infrastructure gets built where.
insights.quote: In regions with lower-than-average pipeline costs, pipelines may have a clear advantage over alternative methods, such as shipping.
insights.locator: Discussion, third implication

themes.theme: Country risk and cost of capital as a cost driver

insights.claim: Most hydrogen transport studies assume a single uniform weighted average cost of capital of 4-6% across all countries, implicitly pricing investor risk identically in every jurisdiction a pipeline crosses.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Uniform-WACC hydrogen cost curves systematically flatter emerging-market export projects; adjust delivered cost estimates for real country risk.
insights.quote: This assumption implies a uniform investor risk across national borders
insights.locator: Methods, 'WACC' subsection

insights.claim: Country-specific WACCs applied across 4,934 route observations span 4.7% to 20.7% with a median of 6.6% and an interquartile range of 5.4% to 8.5%, so the financing cost input alone varies more than fourfold.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Country risk premium, not construction cost, can be the swing variable in emerging-market hydrogen export economics; de-risking instruments are the lever.
insights.locator: Fig. 6 caption: 'minimum–maximum, 4.7–20.7%; median, 6.6%'

insights.claim: The WACC is decomposed into a country-independent mature-market equity risk component of 4.72% plus a country-specific premium capturing economic, financial, social, political and legal risk, sourced from Damodaran's equity risk premium data.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Gives a transparent, replicable way to reprice any hydrogen corridor for sovereign risk using publicly available ERP data.
insights.locator: Methods, 'WACC' subsection

insights.claim: Adding geographic factors widens the cost distribution and adding country-specific WACC widens it further at both ends, yet the modal cost stays near 15 EUR/MWh per 1,000 km, so the conventional approach gets the central case roughly right while erasing the tails that matter for project selection.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Explains why simplistic models look fine in aggregate but mislead on individual investment decisions — the error lives in the tails.
insights.quote: In all three steps, the ‘peak’ LCOT stays the same at around 15 €/MWhH2,LHV/1000kmstraight-line, but the distribution spreads more with each step.
insights.locator: Section 'Country-specific WACCs further increase the range of costs'

insights.claim: The country-risk approach deliberately omits offsetting advantages in emerging markets such as lower labour costs and simpler permitting, which means the modelled penalty on developing-country corridors is likely overstated.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A known directional bias in the results; real emerging-market corridor costs may be better than the model implies.
insights.locator: Methods, 'WACC' subsection: 'it neglects advantages such as lower labour costs'

insights.claim: A 2,909 km Benin-to-Algeria route achieves a total factor of 1.02, essentially free of detour or terrain penalty, because barren and savannah land, low population density and existing Algerian pipeline corridors impose no extra cost.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Trans-Saharan corridors are the cheapest per-km hydrogen routes modelled; a structural argument for North African export to Europe via pipeline.
insights.locator: Fig. 5 discussion: 'Route a, connecting Benin to Algeria, has a total factor of 1.02'

insights.claim: A Fujian-to-Shanghai route in China detours almost not at all (factor 1.06) yet carries a cost factor of 2.21 and a total factor of 2.35 because of uneven terrain, mixed cropland and forest, offshore segments and dense population along the corridor.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Chinese coastal industrial hydrogen links cost roughly double the naive estimate; a short route is not a cheap route.
insights.locator: Fig. 5 discussion: 'Route b, connecting Fujian with Shanghai in China'

insights.claim: A South Brazil-to-Chile route routes deliberately through the Andes and the Atacama Desert to avoid costlier Argentine terrain, keeping the cost factor at 1.15 but pushing the detour factor to 1.65 for a total factor of 1.91.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The Atacama is flagged as a region with good hydrogen supply potential, but its export corridors carry a ~90% cost premium over the straight line.
insights.locator: Fig. 5 discussion: 'Route c connects South Brazil and Chile'

insights.claim: A Sumatra-to-Sri Lanka link cannot cross the Bay of Bengal directly because depths exceed 3,000 m, forcing a mainland detour past Myanmar, Bangladesh and India that more than doubles the distance for a total factor of 2.78.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Bathymetry hard-rules out many intuitive Asian hydrogen pipeline links, pushing that trade toward shipped carriers by default.
insights.quote: The deep waters of the Bay of Bengal, reaching depths of more than 3,000 m, prevent the construction of an offshore pipeline along the straight-line route.
insights.locator: Fig. 5 discussion: 'For route d, connecting Sumatra, Indonesia, to Sri Lanka'

themes.theme: Trade-flow consequences in energy system models

insights.claim: Replacing a uniform 1.2 detour factor with route-specific costs changes hydrogen flows on at least 83% and up to 93% of used pipeline corridors across five European scenarios, even though transport is only a small share of total hydrogen supply cost.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Small input errors in transport cost produce large swings in which corridors get built; existing European hydrogen network plans are less robust than they look.
insights.quote: at least 83% (E-540) of routes were impacted (change of more than ±1%) by changing the cost assumptions with a maximum of 93%
insights.locator: Section on Fig. 7: 'Figure 7 shows the relative changes in hydrogen flow'

insights.claim: In one scenario half of all hydrogen flows change by more than plus or minus 50% and one corridor reverses direction entirely, with Austria switching from importing hydrogen from the Czech Republic to exporting to it.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Import-versus-export status of individual countries is not robust to a modelling assumption; treat national hydrogen balance forecasts as provisional.
insights.quote: Austria switches from importing from the Czech Republic to exporting to it
insights.locator: Section on Fig. 7: 'In the E-1600 scenario, half of all flows change by more than ±50%'

insights.claim: In three of five scenarios at least one pipeline route is discarded entirely under route-specific costing, and in four of five at least one route more than doubles its flow, so the corridor set itself is unstable.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Stranded-asset risk for specific hydrogen corridors is real; a route that clears in one cost framework disappears in another.
insights.locator: Section on Fig. 7: 'In three out of the five scenarios, at least one route is completely discarded'

insights.claim: The number of used pipeline routes scales with demand, rising from 12 corridors in a 540 TWh European hydrogen demand scenario to 30 in an 1,800 TWh scenario, so network breadth is a direct function of how much industrial demand actually materializes.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Corridor count is a leveraged bet on European hydrogen demand; a low-demand outcome supports less than half the network.
insights.locator: Section on Fig. 7: 'The absolute number of used pipeline routes increases from 12'

insights.claim: The European demand scenarios tested span 540 TWh, representing much of Europe's energy-intensive industry being outsourced, to 2,360 TWh assuming industry plus long-distance heavy-duty freight uptake, a more than fourfold uncertainty range on the demand side alone.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The low case explicitly assumes industrial offshoring — European hydrogen demand and European industrial base are the same bet.
insights.quote: ranging from a low demand of 540 TWhH2,LHV, outsourcing much of Europe’s energy intensive industry, to a high demand of 2,360 TWhH2,LHV
insights.locator: Discussion: 'we analyse the effect of our calculations on the European energy system under five different scenarios'

insights.claim: The direction of the effect is consistent across two independent models and five demand levels, which the authors read as a structural response to route-specific cost inputs rather than a quirk of one model.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Raises confidence that the critique generalizes — it is a flaw in the modelling convention, not in one team's code.
insights.locator: Section on Fig. 7: 'The consistency of our general findings across all five scenarios'

themes.theme: Model mechanics, data assets and limitations

insights.claim: The model discretizes the world into roughly 12.7 million tiles of about 42.5 square kilometres each and runs Dijkstra least-cost routing between 264 regional hubs, producing about 4,900 candidate international pipeline connections.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A reproducible global corridor screening method; the resolution limits it to strategic screening rather than detailed engineering routing.
insights.locator: Methods: 'Geographic characteristics' and 'Country hubs'

insights.claim: Hard exclusions in the cost surface are tiles more than half covered by protected land, ocean deeper than 3,000 m and population density above 4,000 inhabitants per square kilometre, each assigned a prohibitive cost factor of 99.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: These three constraints, not engineering limits, determine which intercontinental hydrogen links are physically routable at all.
insights.locator: Methods, 'Geographic characteristics'

insights.claim: Terrain cost factors run from 1.0 on flat ground to 4.0 on steep alpine slopes and land-use factors from 1.0 to 5.0 across eleven categories, while corridors with existing oil and gas pipeline infrastructure receive an outright cost discount.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Quantifies why brownfield gas corridors are the cheap option — co-location with legacy infrastructure is a direct capex discount, not just a permitting convenience.
insights.locator: Methods, 'Geographic characteristics'

insights.claim: Economics assume a uniform 0.9 m pipeline diameter, fixed O&M at 5% of capex, recompression from 30 to 100 bar every 250 km and a 2020 cost base, so results are comparative rather than project-specific.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Do not lift these LCOT numbers into a project model without resizing diameter to actual throughput and updating the 2020 cost base for steel inflation.
insights.locator: Methods: 'Cost calculation' and 'Distance-specific pipeline cost and base cost'

insights.claim: The analysis explicitly excludes the repurposing of existing gas pipelines for hydrogen, which is the cheapest route to hydrogen transport capacity and the backbone of most European network plans.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The biggest gap in the results — real European corridor costs will be materially lower where conversion of existing gas lines is viable.
insights.locator: Main and Conclusion: 'the exclusion of existing pipeline repurposing are discussed in Supplementary Note 1'

insights.claim: The authors deliberately refrain from modelling hydrogen-specific policy measures in order to keep a globally comparable level-playing-field cost estimate, meaning subsidies and hydrogen-specific incentives are absent from every number reported.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: These are unsubsidized costs; real project economics in the EU, US or Japan will differ by the size of the local support scheme.
insights.quote: We refrain from modelling hydrogen-specific policy measures to maintain globally comparable, ‘level‑playing‑field’ cost estimates.
insights.locator: Main: 'We capture the political dimension by using country-specific WACCs'

insights.claim: The full route and cost dataset is released openly on Zenodo and the routing model is published as an interactive tool called HyTROM hosted by Fraunhofer, letting any stakeholder compute custom corridors with their own assumptions.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
entities: Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research ISI
insights.so_what: A free, auditable due-diligence tool for screening any proposed hydrogen corridor against an independent cost baseline.
insights.locator: Data availability and Code availability sections

insights.claim: The work was funded by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research through the HYPAT and HySecunda projects, tying the analysis to Germany's programme for assessing hydrogen import partnerships including with southern Africa.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
entities: German Federal Ministry of Education and Research
Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research ISI
insights.so_what: Signals where German import-corridor policy analysis is being generated; HYPAT outputs tend to precede German hydrogen partnership decisions.
insights.locator: Funding section

insights.claim: Robustness is tested by raising WACC uniformly by one to three percentage points and by inflating each geographic cost-factor group by 20%, an explicit acknowledgement that project-specific hydrogen risk premiums above the country baseline were not in the base case.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Base-case costs are a floor; hydrogen-specific project risk sits on top of the country WACC and pushes delivered costs higher.
insights.locator: Methods, 'Sensitivity analyses'

insights.claim: Future work is flagged as needing to model the influence of political relationships on trade dynamics and shared pipeline use among multiple hubs, meaning bilateral geopolitics is currently proxied only by a country risk premium.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Corridor viability in practice will hinge on alliances and transit-country leverage that no current cost model captures.
insights.locator: Conclusion: 'Future research should address the limitations identified in this study'
